It covers:
1. Joint and marginal probabilities (thinking about $Pr(A \cap B)$ versus $Pr(A)$ and $Pr(B)$).
2. Intersection: “both events happen,” written $A \cap B$.
3. Union of events: “at least one happens,” written $A \cup B$ (and the union rule idea).
4. Mutually exclusive events and exhaustive events, plus the complement rule.
5. Conditional probability, defined as

$$

$$

6. Bayes’ rule as a way to relate conditional probabilities (turning $Pr(A \mid B)$ into something involving $Pr(B \mid A)$ and base rates).

Pre-recorded lecture 1 is about BASIC PROBABILITY FOR MULTIPLE EVENTS.

Core objects are events (subsets of the sample space $S$), and how to combine them:

1. Joint probability (intersection):

$$
P(A \cap B)
$$

2. Marginal probability:

$$
P(A)
$$

3. Union (either event happens) and the union rule:

$$
P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B)
$$

4. Special cases: mutually exclusive events (then $P(A \cap B)=0$) and complements:

$$
P(A^c)=1-P(A)
$$

Then it moves to CONDITIONAL PROBABILITY and Bayes’ rule, with the key definition:

$$
P(A|B)=\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}
$$

Interactive Lecture 8 is about DIFFERENCE IN DIFFERENCES (DiD) as a “middle way” causal inference method using observational data.

Core idea: compare a treated group and a comparison group BEFORE and AFTER a policy or intervention, then subtract out the common time trend.

The key estimand is the DiD contrast:

$$\text{DiD} = \left(\bar{Y}_{T,post}-\bar{Y}_{T,pre}\right)-\left(\bar{Y}_{C,post}-\bar{Y}_{C,pre}\right)$$

It’s framed alongside other design-based regression strategies (Regression Discontinuity and Instrumental Variables) and emphasizes the main limitation: whether the identifying assumption is credible in your setting. For DiD, the central assumption is PARALLEL TRENDS: absent treatment, the treated group would have followed the same change over time as the comparison group (the “unobserved counterfactual trend” shown in the graphs).

One of the motivating examples is policy-type questions like minimum wage changes (the burger-flipping robot slide is hinting at firms adjusting technology/employment), where DiD is commonly used by comparing affected vs less-affected groups over time.

Interactive Lecture 8 is about DIFFERENCE-IN-DIFFERENCES (DiD) as a quasi-experimental research design.

Core idea: compare a treated group and a control group BEFORE vs AFTER a policy/intervention, and take the “difference of differences”:

$$\text{DiD} = (\bar Y_{T,\text{post}}-\bar Y_{T,\text{pre}}) - (\bar Y_{C,\text{post}}-\bar Y_{C,\text{pre}})$$

Key identifying assumption is PARALLEL TRENDS: absent the intervention, the treated group would have followed the same trend as the control group (the unobserved counterfactual line in the lecture’s graph).

It also connects DiD to a regression with an interaction:

$$Y_{it}=\alpha+\beta(Treat_i \times Post_t)+\gamma Treat_i+\delta Post_t+u_{it}$$

where $\beta$ is the DiD estimate.

Exhaustive events are a set of events that together cover the entire sample space, so at least one of them must happen.

Formally, events $A,B,\dots,C$ are EXHAUSTIVE if

$$\Pr(A\cup B\cup \dots \cup C)=1$$

Common special case: an event and its complement are always exhaustive. If $A^c$ is “not $A$,” then

$$A\cup A^c=\Omega \quad \Rightarrow \quad \Pr(A\cup A^c)=1$$

and that implies the complement rule:

$$\Pr(A^c)=1-\Pr(A)$$

The course materials for Interactive Lecture 3 are organized around the idea “THE SAMPLE IS NOT THE POPULATION”: the population has fixed parameters (like a true mean $\mu$), while the sample you draw is random, so any statistic you compute from it is a random variable.

The key object is the sample mean:

$$
\bar{X}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i
$$

and the point is that $\bar{X}_N$ varies from sample to sample even when the population mean $\mu = E[X_i]$ is fixed. That distinction sets up why we care about properties like “unbiasedness”:

$$
\text{Unbiased: } E[\hat{\theta}] = \theta
$$

Cournot quantity competition: firms choose quantities simultaneously, then the market price adjusts to clear demand given total output.

Set up (duopoly from the course materials). Firm $i$ chooses $q_i$ taking rival output $q_j$ as given. With inverse demand $P(Q)$ where $Q=q_1+q_2$, profit is

$$
\pi_i(q_i,q_j)=q_i P(q_i+q_j)-C_i(q_i)
$$

Firm $i$’s best response comes from the first-order condition

$$
\frac{\partial \pi_i}{\partial q_i}=P(Q)+q_i P'(Q)-MC_i(q_i)=0
$$

Example (linear demand, constant marginal cost). Suppose

$$
P(Q)=a-bQ,\quad C_i(q_i)=cq_i
$$

Then

$$
\pi_i=q_i\bigl(a-b(q_i+q_j)\bigr)-cq_i
$$

Differentiate with respect to $q_i$ and set to zero to get firm $i$’s reaction function $q_i=BR_i(q_j)$. Can you take that derivative and simplify it into a formula for $q_i$ as a function of $q_j$?

In plain Cournot, firms choose quantities SIMULTANEOUSLY, so there isn’t a “first mover” inside the model; first-mover advantage is a Stackelberg (sequential quantity) idea.

What timing does your setup assume: do firms pick $q_1$ and $q_2$ at the same time (Cournot), or does firm 1 pick $q_1$ first and firm 2 observe it and then pick $q_2$ (Stackelberg)?

Repeated interactions change Cournot because a firm’s objective becomes discounted LIFETIME profit, not just today’s profit:

$$
V_i=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\delta^t \pi_i^t
$$

where $\delta$ is the probability the game continues (equivalently, how much firms value the future).

In the one-shot Cournot stage game, deviation incentives are checked ONLY against current-period payoffs; in the repeated version, deviation can trigger future “punishments” that reduce later profits, which can make more cooperative quantities sustainable.

A DCF values a firm as the present value of expected free cash flows plus a terminal value:

$$V_0=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{FCF_t}{(1+WACC)^t}+\frac{TV_T}{(1+WACC)^T}$$

Build it in this order:
1. Forecast operating performance to get EBIT, then compute

$$NOPAT_t=EBIT_t(1-\tau)$$

2. Convert accounting profits to free cash flow:

$$FCF_t=NOPAT_t-\Delta WC_t + D\&A_t - Capex_t$$

Circular flow is the basic macro “model” showing how HOUSEHOLDS and FIRMS interact in two markets, with a REAL flow and a MONETARY flow.

1) Two markets
1. Product (goods and services) market: firms sell goods and services to households.
2. Factor (inputs/resources) market: households sell labor, land, capital, entrepreneurship to firms.

2) Two flows happening at the same time
1. Real flow: households provide factors to firms, firms produce goods and services, households consume them.
2. Monetary flow: firms pay households income for factors (wages, rent, interest, profit), households use that income to pay firms for goods and services.

3) The key accounting identity in this simple model
Because the course materials assume no government, no trade, and households spend all income on consumption:

$$Y = \text{Income} = \text{Expenditure} = \text{Value of Output}$$

and in this stripped-down economy,

$$Y = C.$$

First step to check your understanding: in the factor market, who is the SELLER and who is the BUYER of labor?

2) Nominal GDP (each year)
Use current-year prices and quantities:

$$
Y_t = \sum_i P_{i,t} Q_{i,t}
$$

Here $i \in \{\text{Food, Clothes}\}$. Percentage change from year $t-1$ to $t$ is

$$
\%\Delta Y_t = \frac{Y_t - Y_{t-1}}{Y_{t-1}} \times 100
$$

3) Real GDP (pick a base year $b$)
Hold prices fixed at base-year prices:

$$
y_t^{(b)} = \sum_i P_{i,b} Q_{i,t}
$$

4) GDP deflator
By definition,

$$
\text{Deflator}_t = \frac{Y_t}{y_t^{(b)}} \times 100
$$

5) CPI (pick a basket year, usually the same base year $b$)
Fix quantities at the basket’s quantities:

$$
\text{CPI}_t = \frac{\sum_i P_{i,t} Q_{i,b}}{\sum_i P_{i,b} Q_{i,b}} \times 100
$$

6) “Which years exhibit growth?”
In this setup, “growth” means real output rising, so you look at the percent change in REAL GDP (not nominal, which mixes output and price changes).
